notes.meaning: God gives Moses a new set of rules to pass on. They are for Aaron and his sons, the priests, and also for all the people, because both groups had to keep them. The goal was to stop Israel from going back to the false worship they had learned in Egypt.

An Israelite who killed an ox, lamb, or goat had to bring it to the Tent of Meeting. If he did not, he was guilty of shedding blood, almost as if he had killed a person, and he was to be "cut off" from God's people. Being cut off meant removal from the community, carried out either by the judges or by God Himself. Bible teachers differ on how far this went. Some think that in the wilderness it covered every animal killed for food. Others think it covered only animals killed as sacrifices. Either way, the rule was later changed for daily meat once Israel lived spread out in Canaan (Deuteronomy 12).

Here is the reason for the rule. People had been offering sacrifices out in the open fields, a habit they picked up in Egypt. Now they must bring them to the priest at the tent as peace offerings. A peace offering was a sacrifice that was partly eaten by the worshiper as a shared meal before God. Peace offerings were the most common kind, so the temptation to offer them privately was strongest.

The priest, not the ordinary worshiper, was to sprinkle the blood on God's altar and burn the fat. The blood and the fat belonged to God in a special way, and this offering pleased Him. Keeping sacrifice in the priests' hands also kept worship done God's way.

The "goat demons" were false gods pictured as hairy goats. A goat-god of this kind was worshipped in Egypt. Behind such idols stands the devil, so offering to them was really offering to demons (compare 1 Corinthians 10:20). Chasing them is called prostitution because Israel was bound to God like a wife to her husband, and idol worship broke that bond. The "permanent statute" is the lasting rule that sacrifice belongs to the LORD alone.

The same law covered foreigners living among Israel who had joined their faith. No burnt offering or sacrifice could be made anywhere except at the tent. This kept people away from pagan altars in the fields and groves. It also kept worship under the priests' care and united the people around one altar. For Christians, worship is not tied to one place, because Christ Himself is our altar, and our offerings are welcome to God through Him alone.

Eating blood was strictly forbidden for Israelites and for foreigners who had joined them. God says He will "set His face against" such a person. That means He will judge them Himself. Eating blood could easily be done in secret, so even if the courts never found out, God would. Pagans of that time drank blood in their worship, and this law also guarded against that.

This is the heart of the chapter. An animal's life is in its blood, and God set that blood apart for the altar to make atonement, which means covering sin and making peace with God. A sinner deserved to die. God accepted the life of an animal in the sinner's place. These sacrifices pointed ahead to Christ, whose shed blood truly makes atonement. So the blood was given for something far better than food.

Because blood was set apart for atonement, God repeats the ban for Israelites and for foreigners among them. Many older Protestant teachers say this was part of the ceremonial law, which pointed to Christ and ended with His coming. The early church's rule against blood in Acts 15 was meant for a short time, to avoid offending Jewish believers. What lasts is the call to treat Christ's blood with deep respect, never as something common.

Hunted animals that were allowed as food could not be brought to the altar. Their blood still had to be drained and covered with dirt. Pagan hunters poured out blood as an offering to a hunting god. Covering it gave the blood a respectful burial and kept it from any such use.

God gives the reason again: the life of every creature is in its blood. Anyone who eats it is cut off. The law also taught God's people to value the life of animals and not to be cruel or bloodthirsty.

An animal that died by itself or was killed by wild beasts still had its blood in it. Someone who ate it, likely without thinking, had to wash his clothes and bathe. He stayed "unclean" until evening, which means not fit to take part in worship. The "foreigner" here means someone who had joined Israel's faith. Other outsiders were allowed to eat such meat (Deuteronomy 14:21).

If he refused to wash, he would "bear his iniquity." That means he carried his guilt and its punishment, and he needed to offer a sacrifice for it. God had given a simple way to be cleansed. Turning it down added a new sin to the old one.
